traveler: San Antonio Abad (Antony the Great, Antonios of Coma)
title: The Inner Mountain: the Fort at Pispir, the Two Sheepskins, and the Grave Nobody Found
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Village of Coma and the Gospel Read Aloud

stops.name: Coma, born to landowning Christians in Middle Egypt
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius gives no birth year; 251 is the standard chronology, and the 12 January date attached to it in modern reference works is a back-formation from the feast day.
stops.campa: A son is born in Middle Egypt to Christian parents who own land and work it, some thirty kilometres north-east of Herakleopolis Magna. Athanasius, who will write his life, says only that he is by descent an Egyptian, of a family with land and standing. The name of the village, Coma, reaches us through Sozomen and later tradition; the Life itself never gives it. His parents keep him out of the Greek schools and out of the company of other children. He learns to read in church, and reads nothing else.
suggested_refs: Qiman al-Arus, Beni Suef Governorate, the modern identification of the village of Coma

stops.name: Coma, the parents dead and a sister to keep
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius gives his age as about eighteen or twenty and no year at all; 269 is arithmetic from the reconstructed birth date.
stops.campa: Both parents die within a short time of each other, and Antony, eighteen or twenty years old, is left with the estate and with one younger sister, unmarried and in his charge. He keeps the house going for about six months. Athanasius has him walking to church and back in these months, thinking about the apostles who left everything, and about the believers in Acts who sold their possessions and laid the price at the apostles' feet. Nothing has happened yet. He is a young landowner with a sister to settle and a decision he has not made.
suggested_refs: The Herakleopolite nome, the agricultural district that supported the family estate

stops.name: The village church, the Gospel read twice
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius dates nothing here; c.270 is reconstructed from the interval he gives after the parents' death.
stops.campa: He walks into the church while the Gospel is being read and hears the words spoken to the rich young man. He takes the reading as addressed to himself, walks out, and signs the family land over to the villagers so that neither he nor his sister will ever be troubled about it. Months later a second reading, take no thought for tomorrow, empties the house of what remains. He sells the movable goods, gives the money to the poor, keeps a little back for his sister, then gives that away too.
stops.quote: go, sell that thou hast, and give to the poor
stops.quote_source: Matthew 19:21 as quoted at Athanasius, Life of Antony 2
suggested_refs: The parish church of Coma, where both readings were heard

stops.name: The next village, apprenticed to an old man
stops.date_confidence: Undated in Athanasius; the roughly fifteen-year span before the fort is reconstructed from his narrative sequence.
stops.campa: He places his sister with a household of known and faithful virgins and takes up the discipline at the edge of his own village, under an old man who has practiced solitude there since his youth. There is no rule to follow and no monastery in Egypt to enter. He works with his hands, eats bread and salt, and when he hears of a good man anywhere in the district he goes to him and takes one thing away: this one's fasting, that one's patience, another's way of holding his temper. Fifteen years pass at it. Athanasius covers them in a paragraph.
stops.quote: if he heard of a good man anywhere, like the prudent bee, he went forth and sought him
suggested_refs: The community of consecrated virgins to which his sister was entrusted, the earliest such house named in the Life

stops.name: The tombs outside Coma, the night of the beasts
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius narrates the episode without a calendar date; the year is an approximation inside the village period.
stops.campa: He has himself shut into a rock-cut tomb outside the village and asks a friend to bring bread at intervals. What comes for him there, in Athanasius's telling, comes with teeth: lions, bears, leopards, bulls, serpents, asps, scorpions and wolves, each in its own shape and each making its own noise. He is found on the floor in the morning, beaten and unable to speak, and is carried to the village church. When he wakes he asks to be carried back. Two and a half centuries earlier Jesus kept forty days in the wilderness above Jericho on the same errand.
suggested_refs: The rock-cut tombs of the Herakleopolite necropolis, reused as ascetic cells
sources: jesus.journey.json (the temptation in the wilderness, 29 CE)

segments.name: The Fort at Pispir: Twenty Years Behind a Wall

stops.name: The east bank at Pispir, walling himself into a ruin
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius gives no year; c.285-286 is the common reconstruction, which puts him at about thirty-five.
stops.campa: At about thirty-five he crosses the Nile eastward to a deserted Roman fort on the far bank, full of creeping things that clear out the day he enters. He stores six months of loaves, carries in water, and builds up the entrance behind him with stone. Nobody seals him in; he does it himself. Twice a year bread is let down to him from above by men who never see his face. Athanasius says he did not go out, and those who came did not see him, for nearly twenty years.
stops.quote: he built up the entrance completely, having stored up loaves for six months
suggested_refs: Deir al-Maymun on the east bank of the Nile, the site identified as Pispir (Wikidata Q12212334)

stops.name: Pispir, twenty years of not being seen
stops.date_confidence: A mid-point inside the roughly twenty-year enclosure; Athanasius supplies the duration, never the years.
stops.campa: Visitors camp outside the wall and listen. What they hear, Athanasius reports, sounds like crowds inside, shouting and wailing and crying out, and they take it for demons and call to Antony through the stone. He does not answer them. He is thirty-five when the door goes up and fifty-five when it comes down, and of what happens in between the only witness is a man who told a bishop about it afterwards. The desert around the fort is at this point empty of monks. There is nobody yet for him to be an example to.
suggested_refs: The abandoned Roman frontier forts of the Egyptian east bank, reused by fourth-century ascetics

stops.name: Pispir, the door wrenched off by his imitators
stops.date_confidence: 305 in most chronologies; the Christian History Institute timeline gives 306, and the one-year discrepancy is left standing.
stops.campa: They come with the intention of copying him, which is not the same thing as coming to see him, and when he will not open they take the door off by force. He walks out. The men who expected a wreck find someone neither swollen from lack of exercise nor shrunk by fasting, exactly as they remembered him before the wall went up, his mind level and his temper even. From that morning he is public property. He never has twenty uninterrupted years again.
stops.quote: when many were eager and wishful to imitate his discipline, and his acquaintances came and began to cast down and wrench off the door by force
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony 14, the emergence from the fort, the text that founds the monastic topos of the unwasted ascetic
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Antony and the Desert Fathers Timeline'

stops.name: Pispir, the cells fill and the outer mountain has a father
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius narrates the gathering as a consequence rather than as a dated event.
stops.campa: Huts and caves fill up around the ruin with men who want what he has and want to be told how to get it. He writes no rule. He visits, corrects, argues, and talks them down from extremes; Athanasius credits him in these years with healings and with driving out demons, and has him tell everyone within earshot that the cure is prayer and the name of Christ and nothing of his own. The desert is made a city, in the phrase the Life gives it, and the city has one father in it.
stops.quote: just as fish die if they stay too long out of water, so the monks who loiter outside their cells or pass their time with men of the world lose the intensity of inner peace. So like a fish going towards the sea, we must hurry to reach our cell, for fear that if we delay outside we will lose our interior watchfulness.
stops.quote_source: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward, Abba Anthony the Great 10
suggested_refs: The hermit colony of the outer mountain, the first attested cluster of Egyptian anchorites under one father
sources: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward (1975)

segments.name: Alexandria, and the Martyrdom He Was Not Given

stops.name: Alexandria, going down to the martyrs
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius names the persecution as under Maximinus; 311 is the standard historical dating of it.
stops.campa: Under Maximinus the confessors are being sent to the mines and the courts, and Antony leaves the desert for the city to be with them. He serves them in the prisons, follows them to the tribunal, and encourages the condemned on the way to their sentence, wanting plainly, Athanasius says, to be taken with them. Six years earlier, in this same city, the legend of Catherine of Alexandria sends a hermit down out of the desert margin to baptize her. The kind of man that story wants at its edge has been available for about twenty years.
suggested_refs: The Alexandrian mines and prisons of the Maximinian persecution, 311
sources: catherine_alexandria.journey.json (the hermit of the desert margin, 305)

stops.name: Alexandria, the washed cloak in front of the prefect
stops.date_confidence: Undated inside the persecution; Athanasius places it during the same visit.
stops.campa: The judge orders that no monk is to appear in the city or show himself at the tribunal. Every other ascetic hides that day. Antony washes his outer garment, stands the next morning on the steps in front where the governor cannot fail to see him, and waits to be arrested. He is not arrested. Athanasius records the refusal without explaining it and has him wait until the persecution ends before going back to his cell, having failed at the one ambition the Life ever allows him.
suggested_refs: The prefectural tribunal of Alexandria under Maximinus Daia

stops.name: Pispir, back to the cell a known man
stops.date_confidence: Post-311; Athanasius gives no date for the return.
stops.campa: He returns to the outer mountain and to the discipline, but the city has seen him now. Bishops know his name, and governors, and the crowds who begin arriving with sick relatives, with lawsuits, with questions about their dead. The Life has him come back and be daily a martyr to his conscience, since the persecution did not take him. He keeps the cell. The solitude is over. Within a year or two he walks east into open desert to get out from under the queue at his door.
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony 47, on the daily martyrdom of conscience

stops.name: The road east, three days behind the Saracens
stops.date_confidence: 313 in the Christian History Institute timeline and in Wikipedia; Athanasius gives no year.
stops.campa: He asks why he is not left alone and gets, in the Life, an answer: go further in. Saracen traders are crossing toward the Red Sea; he falls in with them and walks three days and three nights behind their camels, east into ground with no wells on it. The track he takes stays a track, and his disciples will walk it for the next forty years. He is going out to be alone. Seventeen centuries later there is a walled monastery, a garden and a pilgrim stair on the spot where he stops.
suggested_refs: The caravan track from the Nile valley to the Gulf of Suez, followed by Saracen traders in the fourth century
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Antony and the Desert Fathers Timeline'

stops.name: Mount Colzim, the water and the palms
stops.date_confidence: Placed in the same year as the withdrawal; Athanasius gives no calendar for the arrival.
stops.campa: He finds a mountain standing over a spring, with a few wild date palms at its foot and forty kilometres of nothing between it and the Gulf of Suez. He stops there. The traders bring him bread when they pass. Athanasius says only that he abode in the mountain alone; the cave partway up the slope that pilgrims climb to today is a later identification and not a line in the Life. He is about sixty-two years old, and this mountain will hold him, on and off, for the remaining forty-three years of his life.
suggested_refs: Mount Colzim in the Galala massif, the inner mountain, later the site of Deir Mar Antonios

stops.name: The inner mountain, wheat and the wild donkeys
stops.date_confidence: A settled habit rather than a dated event; the year is a placeholder inside the span.
stops.campa: So that the men who walk out to see him need not carry his bread across the desert, he breaks a small plot of ground near the spring and sows wheat, and later vegetables for his visitors. Wild donkeys come to the water and start on the crop. Athanasius has him take one of them gently and tell the herd, in words, to do no damage, and insists they never touch it again. A pilgrim in the thirteenth century counts three living springs on the site and a thick grove of palms grown up around the same plot.
stops.quote: Do not trust in your own righteousness, do not worry about the past, but control your tongue and your stomach.
stops.quote_source: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward, Abba Anthony the Great 6
suggested_refs: The spring and garden of the Monastery of Saint Anthony, watered by the same source

stops.name: The desert between the two mountains
stops.date_confidence: A crossing repeated across four decades; the date marks the span rather than an occasion.
stops.campa: The inner mountain is not a second fort. He crosses back to Pispir often enough that Athanasius treats it as habit, and the disciples cross the other way, three days on foot through waterless ground, to put their questions to him. Two mountains and one corridor between them, worn by feet going both ways for forty years. He can be reached at the inner mountain by anyone willing to spend three days and carry his own water. That is the whole of the seclusion.
suggested_refs: The three-day desert crossing between Pispir and Mount Colzim, walked by disciples throughout Antony's later life

stops.name: The inner mountain, the emperors write and he is unimpressed
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius gives no year; 337, the accession of Constantine's sons, is an approximate placement.
stops.campa: Letters arrive from Constantine and from his sons Constantius and Constans, addressing him as a father and asking for an answer. Antony is not sure why he should give one. The monks tell him the emperor is a Christian and that silence would give offence, so he dictates a reply: he commends them for worshipping Christ, advises them not to think much of the present, and reminds them that Christ alone is the true and everlasting king. Athanasius notes that he took no pleasure in the letters and would not have minded never receiving them.
stops.quote: Pay attention to what I tell you: whoever you may be, always have God before your eyes; whatever you do, do it according to the testimony of the holy Scriptures; in whatever place you live, do not easily leave it. Keep these three precepts and you will be saved.
stops.quote_source: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward, Abba Anthony the Great 3
suggested_refs: The seven surviving Letters of Antony, transmitted in Coptic, Georgian, Latin and Arabic
sources: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward (1975)

stops.name: Alexandria, summoned down by the bishops
stops.date_confidence: 338 in the Christian History Institute timeline; some secondary chronologies give 337, and the discrepancy is not resolved here.
stops.campa: The bishops and all the brethren send for him, and the hermit comes down a second time, close to ninety years old, to say in public that the Arians are wrong. He tells the city that the Son of God is not a creature and did not come into being out of nothing, and that to call him a work is to blaspheme. He will not so much as talk with an Arian in the street. Athanasius, whose own position in this quarrel depends on exactly such a witness, records the visit at length and is not a neutral reporter of it.
stops.quote: being summoned by the bishops and all the brethren
suggested_refs: The Arian controversy at Alexandria in the years of Athanasius's exiles
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Antony and the Desert Fathers Timeline'

stops.name: Alexandria, the crowds and the conversions
stops.date_confidence: Same visit; Athanasius gives no day, and by his own account the whole stay lasts only a few days.
stops.campa: Pagans and their priests crowd into the church to see the man from the desert. The sick are brought to him and some go home well. The bishop's party puts him at the front of a doctrinal fight that has emperors in it, and the Egyptian who cannot read Greek and answers through an interpreter turns out to be the most persuasive thing the Nicene side owns. He leaves the city after a few days. Athanasius counts the converts and does not count the arguments.
stops.quote: as many became Christians in those few days as one would have seen made in a year
suggested_refs: The Alexandrian church of the Nicene party during Athanasius's episcopate

stops.name: Nitria, a visit the Life does not record
stops.date_confidence: Given only by the Christian History Institute timeline; Athanasius never places Antony at Nitria at all, so the stop is dated only within the 338 visit.
stops.campa: One modern timeline sends him from Alexandria north-west to the monastic settlements of Nitria before he goes home. Athanasius does not. Nitria enters the Life exactly once, in the account of the monk Amoun, and there the number attached to it is a distance and not a residence. The tradition that Antony spent thirteen years in the Nitrian desert appears to be that one sentence, transmitted badly. This stop is marked because the claim is in circulation, not because the Life supports it.
stops.quote: the distance from Nitria to the mountain where Antony was, was thirteen days' journey
suggested_refs: The monastic settlement of Nitria, modern el-Barnugi, founded by Amoun in Antony's lifetime
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Antony and the Desert Fathers Timeline'
Britannica, 'Saint Anthony of Egypt' (the thirteen-year Nitria variant)

stops.name: Pispir, the philosophers come out to the outer mountain
stops.date_confidence: Undated in Athanasius; placed in the 340s by position in the narrative.
stops.campa: Greeks with an education come out to the outer mountain to make sport of a man who cannot read, and Antony answers them through an interpreter. Which is first, he asks, mind or letters, and which is the cause of which. If the mind comes first, then a sound mind has no need of letters at all. Your books need ink and paper, he tells them; mine is present wherever I am standing. Then he calls forward the people troubled by demons who are already there, and invites the philosophers to cure them with syllogisms.
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony 72-80, the disputation with the Greeks at the outer mountain

segments.name: The Journey to Paul of Thebes

stops.name: The inner mountain, the dream of a better hermit
stops.date_confidence: Jerome supplies no chronology; c.341-342 is conventional, and the secondary summaries consulted split between the two years.
stops.campa: Past ninety, Antony catches himself thinking that no monk has been in the desert longer than he has. Jerome says a dream corrects him that night: there is another, further in, and Antony must go and see him. This episode appears in no line of Athanasius. It belongs to Jerome's Life of Paul the First Hermit, a book written in part to take the title of first monk away from Antony and hand it to someone else, and the editors of the Catholic Encyclopedia decline to treat it as history.
suggested_refs: Jerome, Vita Pauli, written c.375, the earliest rival claim to the founding of the eremitic life
sources: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 7

stops.name: The far desert, the centaur and the satyr on the road
stops.date_confidence: Tradition only; Jerome gives no date and the journey has no chronology attached to it.
stops.campa: He sets out alone across ground he has never crossed. Jerome fills the road with company: a centaur who points the way with his hand and gallops off, and a small horned satyr who brings dates and asks Antony to pray for him, explaining that his people have sent him to beg intercession from a God they hear is coming. Antony walks on. Nothing in this paragraph is offered by Jerome as anything but plain fact, and nothing in it is corroborated by any other source.
suggested_refs: The monstrous races of the Egyptian desert in Jerome's Vita Pauli, later a standard motif of Latin hagiography
sources: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 7-8

stops.name: Paul's cave, the raven brings a whole loaf
stops.date_confidence: Tradition only; Jerome gives no date and the day here is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He finds the cave and the old man inside it, and the two greet each other by name, though nobody has told either one the other's. Paul is a hundred and thirteen. For sixty years a raven has brought him half a loaf of bread each day; that afternoon the bird comes down with a whole one, and Paul observes that the Lord has sent dinner. They talk through the night. Paul asks Antony to walk back and fetch the cloak Athanasius once gave him, so he can be buried in it.
suggested_refs: The Monastery of Saint Paul the Anchorite, built over the traditional cave
sources: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 9-12

stops.name: Paul's cave, the lions dig the grave
stops.date_confidence: Tradition only; one summary gives Paul's death as around 341 and another as 342.
stops.campa: Antony comes back with the cloak and finds Paul dead on his knees, head up and hands raised, still in the shape of prayer. He has nothing to dig with and no strength to dig anyway. Jerome sends two lions out of the desert, which lie down beside the body, roar as though mourning, scrape out a grave with their paws, and then come to Antony with their heads lowered to be blessed. He wraps the old man in Athanasius's cloak and buries him. A monastery stands over the place today and keeps the bones under its church.
suggested_refs: The lions of the Vita Pauli, among the most reproduced scenes in Western hermit iconography
sources: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 13-16
Wikipedia, 'Monastery of Saint Paul the Anchorite'

stops.name: The inner mountain, the palm-leaf tunic twice a year
stops.date_confidence: Tradition only; Jerome supplies no date for the return.
stops.campa: He carries back Paul's tunic, woven out of palm leaves by the old man himself, and wears it, Jerome says, at Easter and at Pentecost and on no other day of the year. He tells his disciples he has seen Elijah and John in the desert, and Paul in Paradise. The two are paired from here on in Christian memory, the finder and the found, their two caves about twenty kilometres apart in a straight line and some eighty by the road that goes round the massif.
suggested_refs: The palm-leaf tunic of Paul of Thebes, worn by Antony at Easter and Pentecost
sources: Jerome, Life of Paul the First Hermit 16

stops.name: Pispir, the last visit to the outer mountain
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius places the farewell shortly before the death, in the same year; the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He comes down to the brothers at the outer mountain to say goodbye and does not pretend it is anything else. He tells them he is going the way of the fathers, gives them the standing instructions once more, and warns them against the Arians and the Meletians. Then he tells them his age. He has been in the desert since he was about twenty and he wants no part of his body kept in Egypt. The monks weep and take hold of him. He leaves anyway, the way a man leaves for a city he means to reach.
stops.quote: I am near a hundred and five years old
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony 89, the farewell address at the outer mountain

stops.name: The inner mountain, the sickness and the bequests
stops.date_confidence: Athanasius says he fell sick a few months after the farewell; the day here is a placeholder inside the death year.
stops.campa: A few months later he falls ill at the inner mountain, with the two disciples who have been up here with him for fifteen years. He divides what he owns, which comes to four things. One sheepskin and the garment he is lying on, given to him new by Athanasius and worn out on him since, go back to Athanasius. The second sheepskin goes to Serapion of Thmuis. The hair shirt the two men keep for themselves. Then he tells them to put him in the ground and tell nobody where.
stops.quote: To Athanasius the bishop give one sheepskin and the garment whereon I am laid, which he himself gave me new, but which with me has grown old. To Serapion the bishop give the other sheepskin, and keep the hair garment yourselves.
suggested_refs: Serapion of Thmuis, correspondent of Athanasius and one of the two named legatees

stops.name: The inner mountain, the death
stops.date_confidence: The year is secure; 17 January is the liturgical feast day later attached to the death and is not a date given by Athanasius.
stops.campa: He forbids them to let anyone carry his body down into Egypt, where the devout keep the bodies of holy men in their houses and wrap them in linen. He has argued against the custom his whole life and has told bishops to stop it, and does not intend to be its next exhibit. Then, in Athanasius's phrase, he draws up his feet as though he sees friends coming for him, and is glad, and dies. The face, they say, is cheerful. He is a hundred and five, of which about eighty-five, by simple subtraction, were spent in the discipline.
stops.quote: this is the great work of a man: always to take the blame for his own sins before God and to expect temptation to his last breath.
stops.quote_source: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward, Abba Anthony the Great 4
suggested_refs: The Egyptian custom of keeping and wrapping the bodies of holy men, argued against by Antony in the Life
sources: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, tr. Benedicta Ward (1975)

stops.name: Near the inner mountain, the grave nobody finds
stops.date_confidence: Immediately after the death; Athanasius gives no interval and no place.
stops.campa: The two of them do exactly what he told them. They wash the body, wrap it, put it in the ground, cover it, and show the place to nobody. Athanasius, writing within a year or two, says plainly that no one knows to this day where it was buried, save those two only. Later traditions will produce the body in Alexandria, in Constantinople, and in a French village in the Dauphine. This pin is a guess at a location that a dying man arranged, deliberately, so that it could never have one.
stops.quote: no one knows to this day where it was buried, save those two only
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony 92, the secret burial, written while the two disciples were still alive

stops.name: Alexandria, Athanasius writes the Life
stops.date_confidence: Composition is dated c.356-360 and is debated among scholars; 357 follows the Christian History Institute timeline.
stops.campa: Monks outside Egypt write to Athanasius asking what sort of man Antony was, and the bishop, who knew him personally, writes it down fast: the parents, the Gospel read aloud, the tombs, the fort, the demons, the twenty years, the two mountains, the death. No Christian life of a man who was not a martyr has been written before it. Within a generation there is hardly a Christian in the Latin west who has not heard of an Egyptian who gave away his fields, and monasteries begin appearing in countries that have no desert at all.
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Vita Antonii, the founding text of Christian hagiography
sources: Christian History Institute, 'Antony and the Desert Fathers Timeline'

stops.name: Antioch, Evagrius puts the Life into Latin
stops.date_confidence: Evagrius finished by 373-374 according to the critical edition; the earlier anonymous translation is undated.
stops.campa: The Life is translated into Latin twice within twenty years of its writing. The first version is anonymous, literal, and survives complete in a single manuscript. The second is made at Antioch by Evagrius, who translates freely for readers who want Latin that reads like Latin, dedicates it to a certain Innocentius, and finishes by about 374. His version survives in roughly a hundred and seventy copies. The oldest surviving manuscript of either is ninth-century, four and a half centuries after the fact.
suggested_refs: Corpus Christianorum, Two early Latin translations of Athanasius' Vita Antonii (2019)
sources: Oxford Cult of Saints database, record E00930

stops.name: Milan, Augustine hears the story in a borrowed room
stops.date_confidence: Augustine places the Milan episode in 386 in the Confessions; he gives no day.
stops.campa: Ponticianus, a countryman of Antony's in the imperial service, calls on Augustine at Milan, sees a book of Paul's epistles on the table, and begins talking about an Egyptian monk whose name Augustine has never heard. He describes the Life, and the two court officials who read it once and walked out of their careers on the spot. Augustine, thirty-two and celebrated and unconverted, hears the story and is ashamed of himself in front of a visitor. He goes out into the garden of the lodging and weeps under a fig tree, and comes back in having decided. He is baptized the following Easter.
suggested_refs: Augustine, Confessions VIII, the visit of Ponticianus and the scene in the garden
sources: Augustine, Confessions, Books VIII-IX (the garden at Milan; the baptism at Easter 387)

stops.name: The Mount of Olives, the cell above Gethsemane
stops.date_confidence: The date follows the margarita_pelagia journey; the Rabia tomb tradition attached to the same chamber is late and undated.
stops.campa: Pelagia of Antioch, who was a dancer, shuts herself in a narrow cell on the Mount of Olives and lives there as a solitary monk under a man's name, in sight of Gethsemane. The vocation is Egyptian, and outside Egypt it is barely forty years old. In the same hillside a domed chamber is venerated, by different people in different centuries, as her grave, as the grave of the prophetess Huldah, and as the grave of Rabia al-Adawiyya of Basra, who kept a hermitage of her own three centuries later.
suggested_refs: The shared domed tomb chamber on the Mount of Olives, claimed by three traditions at once

stops.name: Nitria, the monks come down on Alexandria
stops.date_confidence: The date follows the hypatia journey, which places the Nitrian monks' descent on Alexandria in 414.
stops.campa: Five hundred monks come down out of Nitria to Alexandria to defend their bishop's man Orestes, and the city finds out what the desert has been growing. One of them opens the prefect's head with a stone. The year after, Hypatia is dragged from her carriage and killed by a crowd in the street. Antony has been dead sixty years, never founded Nitria, never lived there, and told everyone who asked him that a monk outside his own cell was a fish out of water.
suggested_refs: The Nitrian monks in the Alexandrian riots of 414-415
sources: The Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Abba Anthony the Great 10

stops.name: Mount Sinai, Justinian walls in the hermits
stops.date_confidence: Justinian's foundation is dated 548-565; the catherine_alexandria journey pins the same event to 555, and the one-year spread is left as it stands.
stops.campa: Two centuries after Antony's death the emperor Justinian puts a fortress wall around the hermits living at the foot of Mount Sinai, a refuge, the account says, kept since the days of the desert fathers. Inside it the monks will in time find the body of Catherine of Alexandria, carried up the mountain by angels according to her legend. The Egyptian pattern has become architecture. Nine centuries later Francis of Assisi dictates the final Rule of his order at a hermitage his brothers call the Sinai of the Order.
suggested_refs: Saint Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai, walled by Justinian around an existing hermit settlement

stops.name: Alexandria, the relics found by revelation
stops.date_confidence: Byzantine synaxarion tradition; no earlier attestation of the date was found, and a rival version puts the discovery in 361.
stops.campa: Two centuries after two men buried him where nobody would look, a Byzantine tradition has the grave revealed and the body carried to Alexandria. One version puts the discovery in 361, five years after the death; another puts it in 561. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on Antony, which follows Athanasius closely, records no recovery at all, and Coptic tradition holds that the body never left the eastern desert. The claims are set down side by side here because they cannot be reconciled.
suggested_refs: johnsanidopoulos.com, 'The Relics of Saint Anthony the Great' (2013), citing Orthodox synaxarion tradition
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Anthony' (silent on any translation)

stops.name: Constantinople, the bones moved ahead of an army
stops.date_confidence: The source gives 635 as the year of the Saracen conquest of Egypt; the Arab invasion of Egypt in fact began in December 639, and 635 is the year Damascus fell.
stops.campa: The relics are said to be taken from Alexandria to Constantinople to keep them out of the hands of an invading army. There the trail stops. No source consulted here names the ship, the year of arrival, or the church that received them. Between this transfer and the next stage of the story lies a gap of three hundred years in which nothing at all is recorded, and the next witness to speak is a French foundation legend written down by the beneficiaries.
suggested_refs: The Arab conquest of Egypt, 639-642, and the Byzantine evacuation of relics from Alexandria

stops.name: La Motte-Saint-Didier, the bones reach the Dauphine
stops.date_confidence: French tradition dates Jocelin's departure to about 1074; one Orthodox account instead has the relics given to a Jocelin in 980 under Basil II, and neither version is documented.
stops.campa: A knight named Jocelin de Chateauneuf is said to bring the relics out of Byzantine territory to a village in the Dauphine called La Motte-Saint-Didier. It is four hundred years since Giles and Veredemus shared a cave in the gorges of the Gardon, a few days' ride south of here, and made the Egyptian pattern ordinary in Provence. No contemporary record of the journey survives. The village keeps the bones, and will in time take the saint's name outright and drop its own.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, Abbaye de Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, on Jocelin de Chateauneuf and Guigues Didier

stops.name: Saint-Antoine, the fire and the Hospital Brothers
stops.date_confidence: 1095 for the founding, confirmed by Urban II the same year; the healings that prompted it are undated.
stops.campa: Pilgrims arrive at the shrine with a burning gangrene that blackens limbs and takes them off at the joint, and some go home cured. The disease takes the name Saint Anthony's fire; centuries later it will be identified as ergotism, poisoning by a fungus growing in rye. Gaston of Valloire, whose son is among the cured, founds a hospital brotherhood at the shrine in 1095. Honorius III sanctions the order in 1218 and it takes the Rule of Augustine in 1248. At its height it runs about three hundred and seventy hospitals across Europe.
suggested_refs: The Hospital Brothers of Saint Anthony and their tau-cross emblem

stops.name: Acre, the Gate of Saint Anthony
stops.date_confidence: The fall of Acre is attested to the day; the dedication of the gate to Anthony the Great rather than to another Anthony is reconstruction from crusader toponymy.
stops.campa: Jacques de Molay is in the city when it falls, and Guillaume de Beaujeu dies defending the gate the crusaders named for Saint Anthony. Whichever Anthony they meant, the hermit's name is on the walls of a Levantine port in an age when his order runs hospitals across Europe under the tau cross and lets its bell-collared pigs forage through town streets to feed the poor it treats. The pig standing beside him in every later painting comes from that privilege, not from Egypt.
suggested_refs: The Gate of Saint Anthony in the walls of crusader Acre
sources: Hospital Brothers of Saint Anthony order history

stops.name: Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, the priory becomes an abbey
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day for the bull of Boniface VIII; the Gothic church, begun about 1280, was not finished for another century and a half, so 1297 is institutional and not architectural.
stops.campa: On the tenth of June Boniface VIII raises the priory to an abbey, makes it the mother house of the Hospitaller order, installs Aymon de Montagne as its first abbot, and removes the Benedictines who had been minding the relics. The Antonines become canons regular and own their own sanctuary at last. The village is by now called Saint-Antoine outright. A man who arranged his own burial so that nobody could find him is the postal address of a French pilgrimage town nine hundred years after his death.
suggested_refs: The bull of Boniface VIII, 10 June 1297, constituting the abbey of Saint-Antoine

stops.name: Arles, the relics deposited at Saint-Julien
stops.date_confidence: The French sources give 9 January 1490; other accounts give 1491 and attribute the move to the Wars of Religion, which did not begin until 1562.
stops.campa: In the course of a custody dispute the monks of Montmajour are said to deposit the relics in the church of Saint-Julien at Arles. Nobody has traced an unbroken chain of custody from that day to any reliquary now standing. At the Revolution the abbey's treasures are sealed up and carted to Grenoble, where they are largely preserved and then forgotten. Whether anything in any of these boxes was ever in the ground near Mount Colzim is a question no source consulted here can answer.
suggested_refs: The church of Saint-Julien at Arles and the Montmajour custody dispute
sources: Regional church history of Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye and Arles

stops.name: Colmar, the altarpiece painted for the patients
stops.date_confidence: Painted 1512-1516 for the Antonine hospital at Isenheim; the panels now hang at the Unterlinden Museum in Colmar.
stops.campa: Matthias Grunewald finishes a folding altarpiece for the Antonine hospital at Isenheim, where men and women are dying of the fire that carries Antony's name. On one wing the hermit is torn at by demons; at the bottom of the panel sits a figure with the swollen belly, the ulcers and the rotting hand of advanced ergotism, painted from the ward. The patients are shown a saint suffering in their own bodies. The other treatment the ward has to offer them is amputation at the joint.
suggested_refs: The Isenheim Altarpiece, Musee Unterlinden, Colmar
sources: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya blog, 'The altarpiece of Saint Anthony the Abbot, ergotism and the antonians'

stops.name: Mount Colzim, the monastery still standing
stops.date_confidence: The eight-year restoration begun in 2002 is documented; the foundation date of the monastery is disputed, with one account dating the buildings to 298-300, which would precede Antony's arrival on the mountain.
stops.campa: The walled compound at the foot of the inner mountain is lived in by Coptic monks who have been raided, massacred in the fifteenth century, cut off, and rebuilt. Inside its church are wall paintings from the thirteenth century, cleaned during an eight-year restoration that cost fourteen and a half million dollars and finished in 2010. Two kilometres away, an hour up a stair cut into the rock, is a cave that tradition and not archaeology calls his. The grave itself has never been found, which was the arrangement.
suggested_refs: Deir Mar Antonios, Red Sea Governorate, and the thirteenth-century Coptic murals of its Church of St Anthony
